item.title: The Complete AI Agent Infrastructure Directory: Runtimes, Sandboxes, Memory, and Identity Projects (2026)
item.description: A curated directory of AI agent infrastructure projects covering runtimes, sandboxes, memory systems, identity, communication protocols, and observability tools for building production-grade agents.
item.content:encoded:
AI agent infrastructure is the shared foundation layer between foundation models and agent applications — encompassing execution environments, communication protocols, memory systems, identity management, durable workflows, observability, and human handoff mechanisms. This curated directory maps the rapidly maturing ecosystem of open-source and managed projects that power production-grade AI agents in 2026, organized across seven critical pillars.

What Is Agent Infrastructure? — Defining the Layer Between Models and Applications

Agent infrastructure refers to the systems, protocols, and platforms that enable AI agents to execute code, persist state, communicate with tools and other agents, manage identity and permissions, recover from failures, and be observed and controlled by humans. It sits below agent frameworks (like LangChain, CrewAI, or AutoGen) and above foundation models (like GPT-4, Claude, or Gemini). While frameworks handle agent logic, orchestration, and prompt management, infrastructure handles the hard systems-level concerns: sandboxed execution, durable state, secure tool access, and production reliability.

The distinction matters because the infrastructure layer is reusable across any framework or model. A well-chosen sandbox, memory system, or identity provider works whether your agent is built with LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, or a custom orchestration loop. As the AI agents market is projected to reach USD 52.62 billion by 2030 at a CAGR of 46.3% (MarketsandMarkets), understanding this infrastructure layer becomes essential for any team deploying agents in production.

The Seven Pillars of Agent Infrastructure

The agent infrastructure ecosystem can be organized into seven distinct but interconnected pillars. Each addresses a fundamental concern that any production agent system must solve.

Execution Environments & Sandboxing — From Process Policies to MicroVMs

Sandboxing is the most foundational infrastructure concern. Every agent that executes code, accesses files, or makes network calls needs an isolated environment. The sandbox isolation spectrum ranges from lightweight process-level policies to full hardware-virtualized microVMs.

Process-level isolation uses operating system primitives like seccomp, AppArmor, and Linux namespaces to restrict what a process can do. This is the lightest-weight approach and is suitable for trusted code or internal automation agents. Container-based isolation (Docker, Podman) provides stronger boundaries with moderate overhead, making it the most common choice for agent sandboxes today. MicroVM isolation (Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor) offers near-VM-level security with container-like startup times, appropriate for untrusted third-party code execution.

Leading projects in this space include:

  • E2B — A managed cloud sandbox platform purpose-built for AI agents. Provides secure cloud environments with filesystem snapshots, package installation, and web server support. E2B’s sandboxes start in milliseconds and support multiple language runtimes.
  • Daytona — An open-source development environment manager that doubles as an agent sandbox. Daytona provides standardized, pre-configured workspaces that agents can spin up on demand, with built-in IDE features and Git integration.
  • Modal — A serverless GPU cloud platform that also serves as an agent execution environment. Modal’s per-second billing and fast cold starts make it suitable for agents that need occasional GPU access for inference or data processing.
  • Ephemeral Sandbox — An open-source project from the Agent Infrastructure Foundation that provides lightweight, disposable sandboxes designed specifically for agent code execution. It emphasizes minimal overhead and fast teardown.
  • Cordium — A managed sandbox platform with built-in network policies, secret management, and audit logging. Cordium targets enterprise deployments where compliance and governance are primary concerns.

The choice of sandbox depends on the trust level of the code being executed. For agents running their own generated code, container isolation is usually sufficient. For agents executing arbitrary third-party code, microVM isolation is the safer choice.

Agent Communication & Coordination — MCP, A2A, and Discovery Protocols

Agents need to communicate with tools, with other agents, and with the systems they control. Two protocols have emerged as the dominant standards in 2025-2026.

MCP (Model Context Protocol), introduced by Anthropic, has become the dominant standard for agent-tool communication. MCP provides a structured way for agents to discover and invoke tools, with official SDKs in TypeScript and Python. A growing ecosystem of MCP servers provides access to databases, APIs, file systems, and web services through a uniform interface. MCP’s key innovation is separating tool definition from tool execution — the agent describes what it needs, and the MCP server handles the actual implementation.

A2A (Agent-to-Agent) Protocol, developed by Google, enables inter-agent communication and discovery. A2A defines how agents can find each other, negotiate capabilities, and exchange structured messages. This is critical for multi-agent systems where specialized agents (a research agent, a coding agent, a review agent) need to collaborate on complex tasks.

Beyond these two protocols, the ecosystem includes:

  • Agent Discovery Registries — Centralized or federated directories where agents can publish their capabilities and find other agents to delegate work to.
  • Message Brokers — Systems like NATS, RabbitMQ, and Kafka adapted for agent-to-agent message passing, providing durability, ordering guarantees, and pub/sub patterns.
  • Tool Registries — Repositories of MCP-compatible tool definitions that agents can discover and use, similar to package registries but for agent capabilities.

Memory, Data & Filesystems — Persistent State and Retrieval for Agents

Agent memory has evolved far beyond simple vector stores. Modern agent memory systems combine multiple retrieval strategies to provide accurate, contextual, and persistent state.

Vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) remain the backbone of semantic search for agents, but they are increasingly supplemented by:

  • BM25 keyword retrieval for exact-match and term-frequency-based search
  • Knowledge graphs for structured relationship queries
  • Fact extraction pipelines that distill conversation history into structured facts
  • Temporal memory that tracks when information was learned and how it has changed

Leading memory projects include:

  • Letta (formerly MemGPT) — An open-source memory system that gives agents “virtual context management” by treating memory as a hierarchical storage system. Letta automatically moves information between working memory, archival storage, and core memory based on recency and relevance.
  • Mem0 — A memory layer for AI agents that provides persistent, personalized memory across sessions. Mem0 extracts facts, preferences, and patterns from agent interactions and makes them available for future conversations.
  • OmniMem — A multi-source memory system that combines vector search, BM25, and knowledge graph retrieval in a unified API. OmniMem is designed for agents that need to query diverse data sources with a single interface.
  • Cortex Memory — A managed memory service with built-in fact extraction, entity resolution, and memory consolidation. Cortex targets production deployments where memory accuracy and consistency are critical.

The trend in agent memory is toward multi-source retrieval — no single retrieval method is sufficient for all use cases, so modern systems combine several approaches behind a unified API.

Identity, Permissions & Trusted Tools — Who Is This Agent and What Can It Do?

Agent identity is the least mature but fastest-growing segment of agent infrastructure. For agents to operate in production, they need verifiable identities, scoped permissions, and auditable access controls.

ThunderID leads the open-source agent identity space with 384 GitHub stars. ThunderID provides an open-source identity stack for AI agents, including credential management, permission scoping, and audit logging. Agents authenticate using ThunderID-issued credentials, and their actions are scoped to specific permissions that can be revoked or modified in real time.

DeepSecure offers a managed identity and security platform for AI agents, with features including:

  • Agent identity issuance and verification
  • Fine-grained permission policies (read-only, scoped write, time-bound access)
  • Real-time threat detection for anomalous agent behavior
  • Integration with existing enterprise IAM systems (Okta, Azure AD, Keycloak)

Agent Identity Protocol (AIP) is an emerging open standard for agent identity that defines how agents prove their identity to tools, services, and other agents. AIP uses cryptographic signatures and verifiable credentials, similar to how TLS certificates work for web servers but adapted for the agent context.

The identity challenge is particularly acute for autonomous agents that need to act on behalf of users. Unlike traditional OAuth flows where a human approves each action, agents need pre-authorized, scoped permissions that can be exercised autonomously within defined boundaries.

Durable Workflows & Recovery — Checkpoints, Retries, and Crash Resilience

Production agents must handle failures gracefully. Durable execution ensures that an agent’s work survives process crashes, network partitions, and infrastructure failures.

LangGraph has emerged as the leading stateful graph runtime for long-running agents. LangGraph provides built-in persistence, checkpointing, and human-in-the-loop capabilities. Agents built with LangGraph can pause execution, wait for human input, and resume from the exact point they stopped — even after a system restart.

Key concepts in durable execution for agents include:

  • Checkpointing — Saving the complete agent state (conversation history, variable values, execution position) at regular intervals or at specific pause points.
  • Retry with backoff — Automatically retrying failed tool calls with exponential backoff, jitter, and configurable max retries.
  • Dead letter queues — Capturing failed tasks for manual review when retries are exhausted.
  • Workflow compensation — Rolling back partial work when a multi-step agent workflow fails mid-way.

Beyond LangGraph, the durable execution landscape includes Temporal (a general-purpose workflow engine adapted for agent use), Inngest (serverless workflow orchestration), and Prefect (data workflow orchestration with agent-friendly APIs).

Observability, Auditability & Provenance — Tracing, Logs, and Replay

You cannot debug what you cannot see. Agent observability has become a critical infrastructure concern as agents grow more autonomous and handle higher-stakes tasks.

RagaAI Catalyst leads the agent observability space with 16K+ GitHub stars. It provides LLM agent monitoring and evaluation, including:

  • End-to-end tracing of agent decision chains
  • LLM call monitoring with latency, cost, and quality metrics
  • Automated evaluation of agent outputs against expected behaviors
  • Drift detection for agent performance over time

OpenLIT is an open-source observability platform for AI agents that provides OpenTelemetry-native tracing, metrics, and logging. OpenLIT’s key advantage is its compatibility with the broader observability ecosystem — it can export traces to Grafana, Datadog, or any OpenTelemetry-compatible backend.

Future AGI offers a managed observability platform specifically designed for multi-agent systems. It provides agent-level dashboards, cross-agent trace correlation, and automated root cause analysis for agent failures.

Arize Phoenix has expanded from LLM observability into full agent observability, adding support for tool call tracing, agent decision logging, and replay debugging.

The observability stack for agents typically includes:

  • Tracing — Recording every step an agent takes, including LLM calls, tool invocations, and decision points
  • Logging — Structured logs with agent context (session ID, step number, intent)
  • Metrics — Aggregated measurements of agent performance (success rate, latency, cost per task)
  • Replay — The ability to replay an agent’s execution step by step for debugging

Human Handoffs & Control — Approvals, Escalation, and Intervention

Even the most autonomous agents need human oversight. The human handoff pillar covers mechanisms for agents to request approval, escalate problems, and accept human intervention.

Key patterns include:

  • Human-in-the-loop approvals — The agent pauses before executing high-risk actions (deployments, financial transactions, data deletion) and waits for human confirmation.
  • Escalation paths — When an agent encounters a situation it cannot handle, it escalates to a human operator with full context of what it tried and why it failed.
  • Intervention points — Human operators can interrupt an agent mid-execution, modify its plan, and resume from the modified state.
  • Audit trails — Every human interaction with the agent is logged for compliance and post-hoc analysis.

Projects in this space include Paperclip (a task management platform for agent-human collaboration), HumanLayer (an API for adding human-in-the-loop to any agent), and built-in handoff capabilities in LangGraph and OpenAI Agents SDK.

Top Agent Runtime Projects — LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Hermes Agent, Goose, OpenHands

Agent runtimes are the execution engines that host and manage agent processes. They handle lifecycle management, state persistence, tool integration, and execution scheduling.

LangGraph (LangChain) — The leading stateful graph runtime with 10K+ GitHub stars. LangGraph models agent workflows as directed graphs where nodes are LLM calls, tool invocations, or decision points, and edges define the flow of control. Built-in persistence, checkpointing, and streaming make it suitable for production deployments.

OpenAI Agents SDK — OpenAI’s official SDK for building and deploying agents. Provides a simple but powerful abstraction for agent definition, tool binding, and handoff between specialized agents. Tightly integrated with OpenAI’s models but supports custom model providers through adapters.

Hermes Agent (Nous Research) — An open-source CLI agent platform designed for autonomous operation. Hermes runs as a persistent agent that can execute code, browse the web, manage files, and interact with APIs. Its skill system allows agents to learn and reuse workflows, and its cron system enables scheduled autonomous operation.

Goose (Block) — An open-source AI agent that runs on your machine with sandboxed code execution. Goose emphasizes developer productivity with built-in code editing, terminal access, and web browsing capabilities.

OpenHands (formerly OpenDevin) — The leading open-source software agent platform with sandboxed execution. OpenHands provides a browser-based IDE for agent interaction, sandboxed code execution, and support for multiple LLM backends. It is particularly strong at software development tasks like code generation, debugging, and refactoring.

Leading Sandbox Solutions — E2B, Daytona, Modal, Ephemeral Sandbox, Cordium

Sandbox solutions provide isolated execution environments for agent code. The choice of sandbox depends on security requirements, performance needs, and operational complexity tolerance.

Solution Type Isolation Level Best For
E2B Managed cloud Container General-purpose agent code execution
Daytona Open-source Container Development environments for coding agents
Modal Managed cloud Container + GPU GPU-accelerated agent workloads
Ephemeral Sandbox Open-source Container Lightweight disposable sandboxes
Cordium Managed cloud MicroVM Enterprise compliance and governance

E2B and Daytona are the leading managed sandbox providers for AI agent code execution, each with different strengths. E2B focuses on simplicity and speed, while Daytona provides richer development environment features. Modal is the best choice when agents need GPU access, and Cordium is the enterprise option for regulated industries.

Memory Systems for Agents — Letta, Mem0, OmniMem, Cortex Memory

Agent memory systems have evolved from simple vector stores to sophisticated multi-source retrieval platforms.

System Type Key Features Best For
Letta Open-source Hierarchical memory, virtual context management Long-running conversational agents
Mem0 Open-source Fact extraction, cross-session persistence Personalized agent experiences
OmniMem Open-source Multi-source retrieval (vector + BM25 + KG) Agents needing diverse data access
Cortex Memory Managed Fact extraction, entity resolution, consolidation Production deployments at scale

The trend is clear: single-method memory is insufficient. The best agent memory systems combine semantic search (vector), keyword retrieval (BM25), and structured query (knowledge graphs) behind a unified API, allowing agents to choose the right retrieval strategy for each query.

Identity and Authorization — ThunderID, DeepSecure, Agent Identity Protocol (AIP)

Agent identity is the fastest-evolving segment of the infrastructure stack, driven by the urgent need for production-ready authentication and authorization.

ThunderID (384 GitHub stars) is the leading open-source identity stack for AI agents. It provides credential management, permission scoping, and audit logging in a self-hosted package. ThunderID is suitable for teams that want full control over their identity infrastructure.

DeepSecure offers a managed identity platform with enterprise features including integration with existing IAM systems, real-time threat detection, and compliance reporting. DeepSecure is the choice for organizations that need SOC 2 or HIPAA-compliant agent identity.

Agent Identity Protocol (AIP) is an emerging standard that defines how agents prove their identity cryptographically. AIP uses verifiable credentials and challenge-response protocols to establish trust between agents and the tools they access.

Observability and Evaluation — RagaAI Catalyst, OpenLIT, Future AGI, Arize Phoenix

Observability is essential for production agent deployments. Without it, debugging agent failures is nearly impossible.

Platform Type Key Features Best For
RagaAI Catalyst Open-source LLM monitoring, agent tracing, evaluation Comprehensive agent observability
OpenLIT Open-source OpenTelemetry-native, Grafana integration Teams already using OpenTelemetry
Future AGI Managed Multi-agent tracing, root cause analysis Complex multi-agent systems
Arize Phoenix Open-source LLM observability, replay debugging Teams transitioning from LLM to agent monitoring

RagaAI Catalyst leads with 16K+ GitHub stars and the most comprehensive feature set for agent-specific observability. OpenLIT is the best choice for teams already invested in the OpenTelemetry ecosystem.

How to Choose the Right Agent Infrastructure Stack — Decision Framework by Use Case

Selecting the right infrastructure depends on your specific use case. Here is a decision framework organized by common scenarios:

Building a coding agent — Start with OpenHands or Goose for the runtime, E2B or Daytona for sandboxed execution, and RagaAI Catalyst for observability. Add ThunderID if the agent needs to access protected resources.

Building a customer support agent — Use LangGraph for the runtime with built-in human handoff, Mem0 for cross-session memory, and OpenLIT for observability. Add MCP servers for CRM and knowledge base integration.

Building a multi-agent research system — Use OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph for orchestration, A2A protocol for inter-agent communication, OmniMem for multi-source memory, and Future AGI for cross-agent observability.

Building an enterprise automation agent — Use LangGraph for durable execution, Cordium for sandboxing with compliance, DeepSecure for identity and access control, and RagaAI Catalyst for comprehensive observability and audit trails.

Building a personal assistant agent — Use Hermes Agent for autonomous operation, Letta for persistent memory, and Ephemeral Sandbox for lightweight code execution.

The Future of Agent Infrastructure — Trends, Gaps, and Opportunities

The agent infrastructure ecosystem is evolving rapidly. Several trends and gaps are worth watching:

Standardization of protocols — MCP and A2A are becoming de facto standards, but the ecosystem still lacks a unified standard for agent identity, memory access, and observability data exchange. Expect consolidation around a smaller number of protocols in 2026-2027.

Convergence of sandbox and runtime — The line between sandbox providers and agent runtimes is blurring. Several projects now offer combined runtime+sandbox solutions, reducing the integration burden for developers.

Agent-native security — Traditional security models assume human operators. Agent-native security models that account for autonomous, high-speed decision-making are an active area of development, with ThunderID and DeepSecure leading the way.

Memory as a service — Managed memory services (Cortex Memory, Mem0 Cloud) are emerging as a category, similar to how managed databases emerged from self-hosted databases. This trend will accelerate as agents need to share memory across sessions and instances.

Observability becoming mandatory — As agents handle higher-stakes tasks, observability is shifting from nice-to-have to must-have. Regulatory requirements for AI agent auditability will drive further investment in this area.

The identity gap — Agent identity remains the least mature pillar. The lack of standardized, production-ready identity solutions is the single biggest blocker for enterprise agent deployment. This represents both a risk and an opportunity for infrastructure providers.

Over 30% of Vercel deployments are now initiated by coding agents, up 1000% from 1.5% in just three months (Vercel Blog). Projects deployed by coding agents are 20x more likely to call AI inference providers than those deployed by humans. These statistics underscore the rapid shift toward agent-driven development and the corresponding need for robust infrastructure.

The AI orchestration market is projected to reach USD 30.23 billion by 2030 from USD 11.02 billion in 2025 (CAGR 22.3%), while the AI platform market is projected to rise from USD 18.22 billion in 2025 to USD 94.31 billion by 2030 (CAGR 38.9%) (MarketsandMarkets). These market projections confirm that agent infrastructure is not a passing trend but a fundamental new layer in the technology stack.

FAQ

Q1: What is the difference between agent infrastructure and agent frameworks? Agent infrastructure handles systems-level concerns like sandboxed execution, durable state, identity, and observability. Agent frameworks handle agent logic, orchestration, prompt management, and tool integration. Infrastructure is reusable across frameworks — a sandbox or memory system works whether your agent uses LangGraph, CrewAI, or a custom loop.

Q2: Which sandbox solution is best for running untrusted agent code? For untrusted third-party code, microVM-based sandboxes like Cordium or Firecracker-based solutions provide the strongest isolation. Container-based sandboxes (E2B, Daytona) are suitable for semi-trusted code but may not provide sufficient isolation for fully untrusted execution.

Q3: How do MCP and A2A protocols differ? MCP (Model Context Protocol) is for agent-to-tool communication — it lets agents discover and invoke tools through a standardized interface. A2A (Agent-to-Agent) Protocol is for agent-to-agent communication — it lets agents find each other, negotiate capabilities, and collaborate. They are complementary and often used together.

Q4: Is agent memory the same as a vector database? No. Vector databases are one component of agent memory, but modern memory systems combine vector search with BM25 keyword retrieval, knowledge graphs, fact extraction pipelines, and temporal tracking. The best systems use multiple retrieval strategies behind a unified API.

Q5: Why is agent identity important for production deployments? Without verifiable identity, you cannot control what an agent can access, audit what it has done, or revoke its permissions when compromised. Agent identity is essential for security, compliance, and accountability in production environments where agents operate autonomously on behalf of users or organizations.

item.title: CubeSandbox: Tencent Cloud's Secure Sandbox Runtime for AI Agents — Full Review
item.description: CubeSandbox is Tencent Cloud's open-source microVM runtime for AI agents with sub-60ms cold starts, hardware isolation, and E2B SDK compatibility.
item.content:encoded:
What is CubeSandbox?

CubeSandbox is an open-source, hardware-isolated sandbox runtime purpose-built for AI agents. Developed by Tencent Cloud and released under the Apache 2.0 license in April 2026, it provides a secure execution environment for LLM-generated code, agent tool calls, and reinforcement learning training workloads. Built on RustVMM and KVM, each sandbox instance boots a dedicated Guest OS kernel in under 60 milliseconds with less than 5 MB of memory overhead, offering hardware-level isolation that container-based approaches cannot match. CubeSandbox is fully compatible with the E2B SDK, meaning developers can switch from E2B to CubeSandbox by changing a single environment variable with zero code modifications.

Why AI Agents Need a New Kind of Sandbox

AI agents today execute code, run shell commands, browse the web, and interact with APIs on behalf of users. Every one of these actions is a potential attack surface. When an LLM generates and executes code, that code may contain unintended side effects — file system access, network calls, or resource exhaustion. Traditional sandboxing approaches like Docker containers share a host kernel, making them vulnerable to container escape exploits. CubeSandbox addresses this by providing a dedicated microVM per sandbox instance, ensuring that even if an agent’s code is compromised, the host system and other sandboxes remain completely isolated.

The Security Problem with LLM-Generated Code

LLM-generated code is inherently unpredictable. Models can hallucinate API calls, generate infinite loops, or produce code that attempts to access restricted resources. In production agent systems, this code runs autonomously — often without human review for every execution. A single malicious or buggy code execution in a shared environment can compromise an entire agent fleet. CubeSandbox’s hardware-level isolation means each agent execution gets its own dedicated kernel, its own virtualized hardware, and its own network stack. If an agent’s code crashes or attempts an exploit, it affects only that single sandbox instance.

Docker vs VM vs MicroVM — The Isolation Spectrum

Technology Isolation Level Boot Time Memory Overhead Kernel Sharing Escape Risk
Docker / Containers OS-level (namespaces) Instant ~1-5 MB Shared host kernel High (CVEs like CVE-2024-21626)
Traditional VMs (QEMU/KVM) Hardware-level 30-60 seconds 128 MB+ Dedicated kernel per VM Very Low
MicroVM (Firecracker) Hardware-level 125-200 ms ~5 MB Dedicated kernel per VM Very Low
CubeSandbox (RustVMM) Hardware-level <60 ms <5 MB Dedicated kernel per VM Very Low

CubeSandbox occupies a unique position: it delivers the isolation of a full virtual machine with the startup speed and memory footprint of a container. This combination is critical for AI agent workloads where sandboxes are created and destroyed at high frequency — sometimes hundreds of thousands per minute.

Architecture Deep Dive

CubeSandbox’s architecture is divided into a control plane and a data plane, with several specialized components handling networking, security, and state management.

Control Plane: CubeAPI, CubeMaster, and WebUI

The control plane manages sandbox lifecycle, scheduling, and user interactions. CubeAPI is the RESTful API layer that accepts sandbox creation, execution, and management requests. CubeMaster is the central scheduler that assigns sandbox instances to available nodes, manages capacity, and handles failover. The WebUI Dashboard provides a graphical interface for monitoring active sandboxes, viewing logs, managing templates, and configuring egress rules. This three-tier control plane architecture mirrors Kubernetes’ design philosophy, making CubeSandbox familiar to DevOps teams already comfortable with cluster management.

Data Plane: Cubelet, CubeHypervisor, and CubeShim

On each host node, the data plane components handle the actual sandbox lifecycle. Cubelet is the node agent that communicates with CubeMaster, similar to kubelet in Kubernetes. CubeHypervisor manages the RustVMM-based microVM instances, handling boot, pause, resume, and teardown. CubeShim provides the OCI-compatible interface that allows CubeSandbox to work with standard container tooling and images. This design means CubeSandbox can use OCI container images as templates, converting them into bootable microVM snapshots.

Network: CubeVS eBPF Virtual Switch

CubeSandbox’s networking layer is built on CubeVS, an eBPF-based virtual switch that provides kernel-level network isolation. CubeVS uses three distinct eBPF programs to enforce network policies: one for ingress filtering, one for egress control, and one for inter-sandbox isolation. This approach achieves near-native network performance while maintaining strict isolation between sandboxes. Egress control rules can be configured per sandbox or per template, allowing administrators to whitelist specific domains or IP ranges that an agent is allowed to contact.

Security: CubeEgress, Credential Vault, and Audit

Security is a first-class concern in CubeSandbox. CubeEgress enforces outbound network policies at the hypervisor level, preventing agents from exfiltrating data to unauthorized destinations. The Credential Vault stores API keys, tokens, and secrets outside the sandbox — secrets never enter the sandbox’s environment variables, filesystem, or process space. Instead, the vault injects credentials directly into authorized API calls at the proxy level. The Audit Trail system records every action within a sandbox session, including which model was called, what code was executed, and the token usage, providing end-to-end accountability for enterprise compliance requirements.

State Management: CubeCoW Snapshot/Clone/Rollback

CubeSandbox uses CubeCoW, a copy-on-write layer built on XFS reflink (FICLONE), to manage sandbox state. Snapshots, clones, and rollbacks all complete in hundreds of milliseconds. This enables powerful workflows: an agent can snapshot its state before a risky operation, clone a sandbox to parallelize testing, or roll back to a known good state after a failure. For RL training workloads, this means thousands of agent environments can be cloned from a single base snapshot in seconds, dramatically reducing the overhead of environment setup.

Key Features and Performance

Sub-60ms Cold Start — How Template Snapshots Work

CubeSandbox achieves its remarkable cold start performance through a three-phase template lifecycle: Init → Boot & Snapshot → Deploy. First, a base template is created from an OCI image. The template is booted once, and a clean snapshot of the booted microVM state is saved. When a new sandbox is requested, CubeSandbox clones this pre-booted snapshot rather than booting from scratch. The result is a fully serviceable sandbox in under 60 milliseconds. Under 50 concurrent creations, CubeSandbox averages 67 ms with a P95 of 90 ms and a P99 of 137 ms. These numbers were measured on Tencent Cloud’s bare-metal lab infrastructure and represent production-grade performance.

Auto-Pause/Resume for Zero Idle Cost

CubeSandbox automatically pauses sandbox instances when they are idle and resumes them in hundreds of milliseconds when activity resumes. This auto-pause/resume feature eliminates the cost of running idle sandboxes, which is particularly important for agent workloads that may have long pauses between tool calls. A single node can support over 2,000 sandbox instances simultaneously, and the auto-pause mechanism ensures that memory is only consumed by actively running sandboxes.

E2B SDK Compatibility — Drop-in Migration

One of CubeSandbox’s most strategic features is its compatibility with the E2B SDK. Developers using E2B’s Code Interpreter SDK can switch to CubeSandbox by changing a single environment variable — no code changes required. This compatibility extends to the sandbox API, file operations, and execution semantics. For teams already invested in the E2B ecosystem, this means they can migrate to CubeSandbox’s hardware-level isolation without rewriting their agent code. It also means CubeSandbox immediately benefits from the entire E2B developer tooling ecosystem.

Template System and Volume Framework

CubeSandbox’s template system allows teams to define reusable sandbox environments from OCI container images. Templates can include pre-installed packages, environment configurations, and network policies. The Volume Framework, introduced in v0.6, allows persistent data volumes to be attached to sandbox instances, enabling stateful agent workloads. Template aliases provide a convenient naming mechanism for managing multiple template versions.

Deployment Options

CubeSandbox supports four deployment modes, ranging from single-node development setups to production Kubernetes clusters.

Single-Node Bare-Metal Setup

For development and testing, CubeSandbox can be deployed on a single bare-metal or virtual machine. The setup requires KVM support and a Linux kernel with eBPF capabilities. This mode is ideal for evaluating CubeSandbox, running local agent tests, or small-scale deployments.

Multi-Node Cluster Deployment

For production workloads, CubeSandbox supports multi-node cluster deployments with CubeMaster coordinating sandbox scheduling across nodes. The cluster mode provides horizontal scaling, high availability, and load balancing. Nodes can be added or removed without disrupting running sandboxes.

Kubernetes Deployment via Helm

CubeSandbox v0.6 introduced native Kubernetes deployment via a Helm chart. This allows teams to deploy CubeSandbox on existing Kubernetes clusters, treating sandbox instances as custom resources managed by the Kubernetes control plane. The Helm chart handles CubeAPI, CubeMaster, Cubelet, and supporting services, integrating with existing Kubernetes networking and storage infrastructure.

Terraform on Tencent Cloud

For teams deploying on Tencent Cloud, CubeSandbox provides a Terraform provider that automates the provisioning of the underlying infrastructure — bare-metal instances, networking, and storage. This is the recommended deployment path for production workloads on Tencent Cloud, as it ensures optimal performance by using Tencent’s optimized hardware and network configurations.

Real-World Use Cases

MiniMax RL Training at 10K+ Concurrency

MiniMax, a leading AI company, uses CubeSandbox’s Agent Runtime for reinforcement learning training at massive scale. According to Tencent Cloud, MiniMax runs RL training workloads with over 10,000 concurrent sandbox instances and million-level throughput, achieving a “zero-incident” security record. For RL training, each training step requires thousands of parallel environment executions, and CubeSandbox’s sub-60ms cold start and snapshot/clone capabilities make it feasible to create and destroy environments at this scale without becoming a training bottleneck.

SWE-bench and Coding Agent Evaluation

CubeSandbox is well-suited for running coding agent benchmarks like SWE-bench, where each test case requires an isolated environment with specific dependencies, file structures, and network configurations. The template system allows each benchmark to define its environment as a template, and the snapshot/rollback feature ensures clean state between test runs. The E2B SDK compatibility means existing SWE-bench runners built on E2B can switch to CubeSandbox with minimal changes.

Enterprise Agent Hosting with Governance

For enterprises deploying AI agents in production, CubeSandbox provides the governance tooling that security teams require. The credential vault ensures that API keys never leak into agent environments. The egress control prevents data exfiltration. The audit trail provides a complete record of every action taken by every agent. Tencent Cloud positions CubeSandbox as an “Agent Runtime” control plane that separates agent state from compute, allowing enterprises to manage agent fleets with the same rigor they apply to their production infrastructure.

CubeSandbox vs The Competition

vs E2B (The Direct Competitor)

Feature CubeSandbox E2B
Isolation Technology RustVMM MicroVM Firecracker MicroVM
Cold Start Time <60 ms ~125 ms
Memory Overhead <5 MB ~5 MB
License Apache 2.0 (Open Source) Proprietary
SDK Compatibility E2B SDK compatible Native SDK
Self-Hosting Yes (multiple deployment options) Limited (E2B Cloud)
Credential Vault Built-in Separate service
Audit Trail Built-in Available in enterprise plan
ARM64 Support Full native support Limited
Kubernetes Deployment Yes (Helm chart) No

CubeSandbox’s open-source nature and self-hosting capabilities give it a significant advantage for enterprises that need to run agent workloads on their own infrastructure. E2B’s advantage lies in its mature ecosystem, broader SDK language support, and managed cloud service.

vs OpenSandbox, Microsandbox, and Daytona

OpenSandbox and Microsandbox are smaller open-source projects that provide container-based sandboxing for AI agents. They lack the hardware-level isolation that CubeSandbox provides, making them suitable for development and testing but potentially insufficient for production security requirements. Daytona is a more established open-source project focused on development environments rather than agent execution, with a different target use case.

vs Firecracker, Kata Containers, and gVisor

Firecracker is the microVM technology that powers AWS Lambda and Fargate. It provides similar hardware-level isolation but lacks the agent-specific features that CubeSandbox offers — credential vault, egress control, audit trails, and E2B SDK compatibility. Kata Containers provides hardware-virtualized containers but has a heavier footprint and slower startup times. gVisor is a user-space kernel that provides a security layer for containers but does not offer true hardware isolation. CubeSandbox’s combination of agent-specific features, sub-60ms startup, and hardware isolation makes it the most complete solution for AI agent workloads.

Pros, Cons, and When to Use It

Pros:

  • Hardware-level isolation with sub-60ms cold starts
  • Open source (Apache 2.0) with no vendor lock-in
  • E2B SDK compatibility enables zero-friction migration
  • Comprehensive security features (credential vault, egress control, audit trails)
  • Multiple deployment options including Kubernetes and Terraform
  • Full ARM64 support
  • Active development with monthly releases

Cons:

  • Relatively new project (April 2026) — ecosystem still maturing
  • Performance benchmarks from Tencent Cloud’s lab, not independently verified
  • Requires KVM-capable hardware — not suitable for all environments
  • Smaller community compared to established projects like Firecracker
  • Documentation primarily in Chinese for some advanced features
  • E2B SDK compatibility may lag behind E2B’s latest API changes

When to use CubeSandbox:

  • You need hardware-level isolation for production AI agent workloads
  • You are running RL training at scale and need fast environment creation
  • You want to self-host agent sandboxes on your own infrastructure
  • You are already using E2B and want to migrate to an open-source alternative
  • You need enterprise-grade audit and governance for agent execution

The Bigger Picture — Agent Infrastructure in 2026

CubeSandbox represents a broader trend in AI infrastructure: the emergence of specialized execution environments for AI agents. Just as Kubernetes became the standard control plane for containerized applications, CubeSandbox and similar projects are vying to become the standard control plane for agentic workloads. The key requirements — hardware isolation, fast startup, state management, and governance — are fundamentally different from both traditional container orchestration and serverless computing.

Tencent Cloud’s decision to open-source CubeSandbox under Apache 2.0 is a strategic move to set de facto standards for agent infrastructure. By making the technology freely available and compatible with the existing E2B ecosystem, Tencent is positioning itself at the center of the agent infrastructure market. The company’s focus on governance tooling — credential management, audit trails, egress control — reflects the enterprise demand for secure, auditable agent deployments.

The open-source strategy also accelerates adoption. With 10,774 GitHub stars and 979 forks in just three months, CubeSandbox has attracted significant community interest. The monthly release cadence (v0.4 in May, v0.5 in June, v0.6 in July 2026) demonstrates active development and rapid feature iteration.

Conclusion and Recommendations

CubeSandbox is a compelling solution for teams that need secure, fast, and scalable sandbox environments for AI agents. Its hardware-level isolation, sub-60ms cold starts, and comprehensive security features make it suitable for production agent workloads, particularly in enterprise environments where security and governance are paramount.

For teams currently using E2B, CubeSandbox offers a migration path that requires minimal code changes, making it worth evaluating as an open-source alternative. For teams building new agent infrastructure, CubeSandbox’s combination of features — credential vault, egress control, audit trails, template system, and multiple deployment options — provides a complete solution that would otherwise require integrating multiple separate tools.

The main caveat is CubeSandbox’s relative youth. The project is only three months old, and while development is active, the ecosystem, documentation, and community support are still maturing. Teams should evaluate CubeSandbox against their specific requirements, particularly around performance, and verify that the benchmarks align with their own infrastructure.

For RL training workloads, enterprise agent hosting, and any scenario requiring hardware-level isolation at scale, CubeSandbox is worth serious consideration. It represents a significant step forward in agent infrastructure and signals the direction the industry is heading.

FAQ

What is CubeSandbox and how does it work?

CubeSandbox is an open-source microVM runtime from Tencent Cloud designed specifically for AI agent execution. It uses RustVMM and KVM to create hardware-isolated sandbox environments that boot in under 60 milliseconds. Each sandbox runs its own dedicated Guest OS kernel, providing stronger isolation than containers while maintaining the startup speed and low memory footprint that agent workloads require.

How does CubeSandbox compare to Docker for AI agent sandboxing?

Docker containers share the host kernel and provide OS-level isolation through namespaces and cgroups, which is vulnerable to container escape exploits. CubeSandbox provides hardware-level isolation with a dedicated kernel per sandbox, making it significantly more secure. While Docker starts instantly, CubeSandbox’s sub-60ms boot time is close enough for most agent workloads, and the security benefits of hardware isolation outweigh the marginal startup time difference.

Is CubeSandbox compatible with E2B’s SDK?

Yes, CubeSandbox is fully compatible with the E2B Code Interpreter SDK. Developers can switch from E2B to CubeSandbox by changing a single environment variable with zero code modifications. This compatibility extends to the sandbox API, file operations, and execution semantics, making migration straightforward for teams already using E2B.

Can CubeSandbox be deployed on Kubernetes?

Yes, CubeSandbox v0.6 introduced native Kubernetes deployment via a Helm chart. The Helm chart handles CubeAPI, CubeMaster, Cubelet, and supporting services, integrating with existing Kubernetes networking and storage infrastructure. CubeSandbox also supports single-node bare-metal deployment, multi-node cluster deployment, and Terraform-based deployment on Tencent Cloud.

What are the hardware requirements for running CubeSandbox?

CubeSandbox requires a Linux host with KVM support and a kernel that supports eBPF. A single node can support over 2,000 sandbox instances. For production deployments, Tencent Cloud recommends bare-metal instances with KVM virtualization extensions. ARM64 is fully supported across compilation, build, and deployment. The memory overhead per sandbox is less than 5 MB, making it efficient even on resource-constrained hosts.

item.title: Agyn Review 2026: Kubernetes-Native Runtime for AI Agent Deployment
item.description: Agyn is an open-source Kubernetes-native runtime for AI agents that combines Terraform-based agent definitions, MCP tool isolation, and zero-trust networking for production agent deployment.
item.content:encoded:
Agyn is an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for AI agents that launched on May 20, 2026, as a complete rebuild from earlier research. It treats AI agents as infrastructure defined through Terraform, isolates credentials at the MCP container level rather than the agent container, and uses OpenZiti zero-trust networking to eliminate VPNs. Unlike agent frameworks that focus on orchestration logic, Agyn solves the infrastructure layer — deployment, scaling, security, and observability — for production agent workloads running on Kubernetes.

What Is Agyn?

Agyn is not another agent framework. It is a Kubernetes-native runtime purpose-built for running AI agents in production. Where frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen focus on how agents reason, plan, and collaborate, Agyn focuses on where and how those agents execute — with proper isolation, governance, and cost control.

The project was introduced on May 20, 2026, through a blog post on agyn.io, accompanied by an academic paper on arXiv (arXiv:2605.27575) published on May 26, 2026, by Nikita Benkovich and Vitalii Valkov. The platform is a complete rewrite from earlier research (arXiv:2602.01465), reflecting lessons learned from real-world agent deployment challenges.

Agyn is licensed under AGPL-3.0, written in TypeScript, and available on GitHub with 217 stars, 5 forks, and 0 open issues as of July 2026. It offers a free Community Edition for self-hosting and enterprise managed services for organizations that want a fully managed experience.

Key Features Deep Dive

Agent Definition as Code via Terraform

The most distinctive feature of Agyn is that agents are defined as Terraform resources. This means your agent configuration — model selection, tool access, environment variables, scaling parameters, and security policies — lives in version-controlled .tf files alongside the rest of your infrastructure.

resource "agyn_agent" "code_reviewer" {
  name    = "code-reviewer"
  image   = "claude-code"
  model   = "claude-sonnet-4"
  tools   = ["github", "slack", "jira"]
  scaling = {
    min_instances = 0
    max_instances = 10
  }
}

This approach brings GitOps workflows to AI agent management. Teams can review agent configuration changes through pull requests, roll back problematic updates, and maintain a complete audit trail of who changed what and when. For organizations already using Terraform for cloud infrastructure, adding agent definitions is a natural extension of existing workflows.

MCP Tool Isolation and Credential Security

Agyn implements a security architecture that separates credentials from agent reasoning. Instead of injecting API keys and service tokens into the agent’s environment — where a compromised or hallucinating agent could expose them — Agyn injects credentials into isolated MCP (Model Context Protocol) containers.

The agent communicates with tools through MCP containers that hold the actual credentials. The model never sees the raw API key or token in its context window. This means:

  • A compromised agent cannot leak credentials — it only has access to tool responses, not the keys themselves
  • Credential rotation is centralized — update credentials in one place, and all agents using that tool inherit the change
  • Least-privilege by default — each tool gets only the permissions it needs, and each agent gets only the tools it needs

This is a significant security differentiator compared to traditional agent deployments where API keys are passed as environment variables directly into the agent process.

Serverless Agent Runtime Model

Agyn uses a serverless execution model where each agent invocation spins a fresh container. There is no warm pool management, no idle compute costs, and no risk of state leaking between invocations.

Aspect Agyn Serverless Traditional Always-On Agents
Compute cost Pay per invocation only Idle compute 24/7
Cold start Sub-second container spin-up N/A (always warm)
State isolation Fresh container per call Shared process space
Scaling Automatic, per-invocation Manual or auto-scaling groups
Resource efficiency Near 100% Often 10-30% utilization

For bursty workloads — the most common pattern for AI agents — this model is significantly more cost-effective. A code review agent that runs 50 times per day costs only the compute time of those 50 invocations, not a 24/7 pod.

Zero-Trust Networking with OpenZiti

Agyn integrates OpenZiti, an open-source zero-trust networking overlay, to handle agent-to-service communication. Instead of opening firewall ports, configuring VPNs, or managing complex network policies, Agyn creates a secure overlay network where agents and services authenticate each other before any traffic flows.

Key benefits:

  • No VPN required — agents running on any Kubernetes cluster can reach internal services securely
  • Mutual TLS — both the agent and the service verify each other’s identity
  • Least-privilege network access — agents can only reach the specific services they are authorized to use
  • No public exposure — services never need a public IP or open port

This is particularly valuable for organizations running agents that need to access internal databases, APIs, or on-premise systems without exposing those systems to the public internet.

Per-Agent and Per-Org Observability

Agyn provides built-in observability for token usage, tool activity, and agent performance at both the individual agent and organizational level. Teams can track:

  • Token consumption per agent, per model, and per time period
  • Tool invocation frequency and success rates
  • Agent execution duration and error rates
  • Cost attribution by team, project, or agent

This observability layer is critical for organizations that need to understand their agent infrastructure costs and usage patterns, especially as the number of agents in an organization grows.

Architecture and Design Principles

Signal-Driven Stateful Serverless Runtime

Agyn’s runtime is built on three architectural principles that address the fundamental challenges of running AI agents at scale.

Signal-driven execution means agents are triggered by events — webhooks, schedule-based cron jobs, API calls, or messages from other agents. This event-driven model aligns naturally with how agents are used in practice: they respond to inputs rather than running continuously.

Stateful serverless is the key innovation. Agyn maintains persistent context that survives container restarts, scaling events, and even multi-region deployments. An agent can be interrupted mid-task, have its container recycled, and resume exactly where it left off. This is achieved through a state store that is decoupled from the compute layer, allowing the stateless container to access persistent state when needed.

Fresh container per invocation ensures that no state leaks between invocations. Each agent call starts with a clean environment, loads the necessary state from the persistent store, executes, and saves any state changes before the container is destroyed.

Agent-Agnostic, Model-Agnostic, Cloud-Agnostic

Agyn is designed to work with any agent, any model, and any cloud. The platform ships with three pre-built agent init images — Claude Code, Codex, and the agn (Agyn’s own agent loop) — but teams can bring their own agent image.

The model-agnostic design means you can switch between OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or open-source models without changing your agent infrastructure. The cloud-agnostic design means Agyn runs on any Kubernetes cluster — AWS EKS, Google GKE, Azure AKS, on-premise, or edge.

Supported Agents — Claude Code, Codex, and Custom

Agyn ships with three pre-built agent init images out of the box:

Agent Image Best For Key Strength
Claude Code Complex reasoning, long-form code generation Anthropic’s Claude model with extended thinking
Codex Fast code generation, IDE-like workflows OpenAI’s Codex with real-time editing
agn Custom agent loops, framework integration Agyn’s own agent loop, fully customizable

Teams can also build custom agent images by extending the base Agyn runtime. This allows organizations to integrate their existing agent frameworks — LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen — into Agyn’s infrastructure layer, getting the best of both worlds: the orchestration logic from the framework and the production infrastructure from Agyn.

Pricing Model — Community Edition vs Enterprise

Agyn follows an open-core business model with two tiers:

Feature Community Edition Enterprise
License AGPL-3.0 Commercial
Self-hosted Yes Yes
Managed service No Yes
Agent definitions Unlimited Unlimited
MCP tool isolation Yes Yes
Zero-trust networking Yes Yes
Observability Per-agent Per-agent + Per-org + Custom dashboards
Fine-grained access control Roadmap Available
Audit logs Roadmap Available
SLA None 99.9% uptime
Support Community Dedicated support team

The Community Edition is free and fully functional for self-hosted deployments. The Enterprise tier adds managed hosting, advanced access control, audit logging, and support SLAs for organizations that need them.

Agyn vs Competitors — How It Differs from LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen

Agyn occupies a different layer of the stack than popular agent frameworks. The comparison is not about which is better — it is about which layer of the problem each tool solves.

Dimension Agyn LangGraph / CrewAI / AutoGen
Layer Infrastructure runtime Agent orchestration framework
Primary concern Deployment, scaling, security, cost Agent reasoning, planning, collaboration
Deployment target Kubernetes Anywhere (but no infra management)
Agent definition Terraform resources Python code
Security model Zero-trust, MCP isolation Application-level only
State management Persistent, decoupled from compute In-memory or manual persistence
Scaling Automatic, per-invocation serverless Manual or application-level
Observability Built-in per-agent and per-org Requires external tools
Networking OpenZiti zero-trust overlay Standard TCP/IP

The two approaches are complementary. Teams can use LangGraph or CrewAI for agent orchestration logic and deploy those agents on Agyn for infrastructure management. Agyn’s custom agent image support makes this integration straightforward.

Use Cases and Real-World Applications

Autonomous Customer Support Swarms

Organizations running customer support at scale can deploy swarms of specialized agents on Agyn — one for billing inquiries, one for technical support, one for account management — each with its own tool access and security boundaries. The serverless model means costs scale with ticket volume, not agent count.

Complex Data Analysis Pipelines

Data analysis agents that process large datasets benefit from Agyn’s stateful serverless model. An agent can be triggered by a new data upload, process the data across multiple invocations (each spinning a fresh container), and persist intermediate results in the state store. The zero-trust networking ensures the agent can access internal databases without exposing them.

CI/CD Code Review Automation

Code review agents running Claude Code or Codex can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines. Each pull request triggers an agent invocation that reviews the code, posts comments, and updates the PR status — all within a fresh, isolated container that is destroyed after the review completes.

Internal Tool Access for Non-Technical Teams

Agyn’s Terraform-based agent definitions make it possible for platform teams to define agents that internal teams can use without writing code. A marketing team might have an agent that can access the CMS, analytics dashboard, and social media scheduler — all secured through MCP tool isolation and zero-trust networking.

Roadmap — Fine-Grained Access Control and Audit Logs

Agyn’s public roadmap includes two major features:

Fine-grained access control will allow organizations to define granular permissions for who can create, modify, and deploy agents. This is essential for enterprises that need to separate development, staging, and production agent environments with different access levels.

Audit logs will provide a complete record of every agent action — what tools were called, what data was accessed, what decisions were made. For regulated industries (finance, healthcare, legal), audit logs are not optional; they are a compliance requirement.

Both features are listed as “coming soon” on the Agyn blog and are expected to ship in late 2026.

Getting Started — Local Bootstrap and Demo Setup

Getting started with Agyn requires a Kubernetes cluster and Terraform installed. The quickstart guide on agyn.io walks through:

  1. Installing the Agyn operator on your Kubernetes cluster
  2. Configuring the Agyn Terraform provider
  3. Defining your first agent as a Terraform resource
  4. Running the agent and observing its output

The Community Edition supports local development with kind (Kubernetes in Docker) or minikube, making it possible to evaluate Agyn on a laptop before deploying to production.

Verdict — Who Should Use Agyn in 2026?

Agyn is a strong choice for organizations that are already running Kubernetes and need to deploy AI agents at scale with proper security, governance, and cost control. It is particularly well-suited for:

  • Platform engineering teams that manage infrastructure for multiple agent workloads
  • Organizations in regulated industries that need audit trails and access control (once roadmap features ship)
  • Teams running bursty agent workloads where always-on agents would waste compute
  • Enterprises with existing Terraform workflows who want to extend GitOps to agent management

Agyn is less suitable for teams that are still experimenting with agents and do not yet need production infrastructure. For those teams, starting with a framework like LangGraph or CrewAI and migrating to Agyn when scale demands it is a reasonable path.

The platform’s AGPL-3.0 license means organizations that want to embed Agyn in proprietary products need to consider the licensing implications, though the Community Edition is free for internal use.

Bottom line: Agyn fills a genuine gap in the AI agent ecosystem. It is not another framework — it is the infrastructure layer that frameworks have been missing. For teams that have outgrown notebook experiments and need to run agents like production services, Agyn is worth a serious look in 2026.

FAQ

What is Agyn and how does it work?

Agyn is an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for AI agents that launched in May 2026. It treats agents as infrastructure defined through Terraform resources, runs each agent invocation in a fresh container, isolates credentials at the MCP container level, and uses OpenZiti zero-trust networking for secure agent-to-service communication.

How is Agyn different from LangGraph or CrewAI?

Agyn operates at the infrastructure layer while LangGraph and CrewAI operate at the orchestration layer. Agyn handles deployment, scaling, security, and observability on Kubernetes. LangGraph and CrewAI handle agent reasoning, planning, and collaboration. The two approaches are complementary and can be used together.

Is Agyn free to use?

Yes, Agyn offers a free Community Edition under AGPL-3.0 that is fully functional for self-hosted deployments. Enterprise managed services with additional features like fine-grained access control, audit logs, and dedicated support are available for organizations that need them.

What agents does Agyn support?

Agyn ships with three pre-built agent init images: Claude Code (for complex reasoning and code generation), Codex (for fast code generation), and agn (Agyn’s own customizable agent loop). Teams can also build and deploy custom agent images.

Does Agyn work with any Kubernetes cluster?

Yes, Agyn is cloud-agnostic and runs on any Kubernetes cluster including AWS EKS, Google GKE, Azure AKS, on-premise deployments, and local development clusters like kind or minikube.
